title: Sliding window
short: Reuse the last answer as a window slides along a list.
what: A window is a run of neighbouring items, like 3 in a row. Instead of adding up every window from scratch, slide it one step: subtract the item that leaves, add the item that enters. The window can also grow and shrink to follow a rule.
analogy: A train passing a platform. As it moves forward one car, one car leaves the platform and one arrives. You only need to look at those two cars to know what is in front of you now.

frames.label: best sum of 3 in a row
frames.say: The first window covers 2, 1, 5. Add them once: 8. That is the best so far.

frames.label: best sum of 3 in a row
frames.say: Slide right. 2 leaves and 1 enters: 8 - 2 + 1 = 7. Two operations, no re-adding.

frames.label: best sum of 3 in a row
frames.say: Slide again. 1 leaves and 3 enters: 7 - 1 + 3 = 9. That beats 8, so best is now 9.

frames.label: best sum of 3 in a row
frames.say: 5 leaves and 2 enters: 9 - 5 + 2 = 6. Lower, so best stays 9. The window hit the end.

frames.label: best sum of 3 in a row
frames.say: The best window is 5, 1, 3. Each slide cost the same small work, so the whole pass is O(n).

when: Subarray or substring of neighbouring items
Best sum or average of k in a row
Longest stretch that follows a rule
Shortest stretch that reaches a total
python:
def best_window(nums, k):
    window = sum(nums[:k])
    best = window
    for i in range(k, len(nums)):
        window += nums[i] - nums[i - k]   # add new, drop old
        best = max(best, window)
    return best

print(best_window([2, 1, 5, 1, 3, 2], 3))
print(best_window([1, 9, 2, 3], 2))
watch: It is for neighbouring items only. Picking any items is a different problem.
For a growing window, move the right edge every step and the left edge only while the rule is broken.
Check the index you drop: with size k, it is nums[i - k].
